# Using Dockerfile-development

`Dockerfile-development` is a dockerfile that is intended to be used with VSCode's [Dev Container extension](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/devcontainers/containers). This lets developers to quickly set up an environment that has the tools used for data preparation and running the web app. It mounts the codebase into the container, meaning the container has access to files outside of it. This allows for development without tearing down and building the container back up again just to see if it worked. This is intended for simultaneous development of data preparation pipelines and web application, but can also be used to work on either one.

## Requirements

- Docker is installed.
- The IDE used must be VSCode, since we need to use the Dev Container extension. If this is not possible, see [below for alternative](#using-without-vscode).
- At least 10GB of free storage for both image and container, and depending on the dataset to be used, another ~24 GB for [data prep](https://github.com/bioinfodlsu/rice-pilaf/wiki/3.5.-Data-Preparation) or ~14 for [only app](https://github.com/bioinfodlsu/rice-pilaf/wiki/1.-Installation). Follow either links to find guides on how to download dataset.
- An internet connection.
- Memory $\geq$ 8GB

## Environment Setup

1. Clone the repo.
2. Open it in VSCode.
3. Download the [Dev Container Extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers)
4. Open Docker Desktop (to wake up the Docker Engine).
4. Open the Command Palette (`Ctrl + Shift + P`) and search `Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in Container`

The Dev Container extension will find the `devcontainer.json` configuration file and will create an image and the container directly (this build step can take a long time since we're downloading tools from the internet). VSCode will present the editor after building. You can now develop as is, with the tools available through the built in terminal.

If it's prefered to use a terminal outside of VSCode, run the following command:
```bash
docker exec -it container-name bash
```

This opens a bash terminal within the container. `container-name` will be randomly generated by Docker. You can find the name in Docker Desktop or running `docker container list` and finding which container corresponds with the generated image by Dev Containers. The image's name will start with `vsc-[folder-name-of-codebase]`.

## Closing and Reopening
To close the environment, simply close VSCode. The container will automatically close on its own. If it doesn't, manually shutting it down is also fine, either through Docker desktop or the console:
```bash
docker stop container-name
```

To reopen the environment, open VSCode and in the Command Palette run `Dev Containers: Reopen in Container`. Sometimes this bugs out, where VSCode attempts to connect and fails indefinitely. I have found that opening Docker Desktop first and manually starting the container and then running the reopen command seems to fix this issue.

## Using without VSCode

If access to VSCode is not possible or undesired, one can manually build the image from the dockerfile and create a container from it. First navigate to the root of the project and run the following:

```bash
docker build -f Dockerfile-develop -t rice-pilaf-dev .
```

This will create an image of the RicePilaf development environment. To create a container with the codebase mounted, run:

```bash
docker run --mount type=bind,src=./,dst=/app --name rice-pilaf-dev rice-pilaf-dev
```

The container will now be running, accessible through:
```bash
docker exec -it rice-pilaf-dev bash
```

You can run commands through this terminal and develop separately using any IDE.

## Some Notes

- Python and pip are orginally installed as  `python3` and `pip3`, but are available as `python` and `pip` because the `python-is-python3` is installed. This is for compatibility with the existing snakefiles, which invoke `python` rather than `python3`. (Which should just be using the `script:` directive rather than turning the scirpts into a command line tool) Wasteful to install? Maybe. But it's the fastest way I could think of doing this. If this offends anyone, feel free to make a PR.
- Because the codebase is now mounted rather than portions being copied over into the container, this breaks some behavior from Dockerfile-worflow. Specifically, it installs ClusterONE and LazyFox into `/prepare_data/workflow/scripts/module_detection`. But since mounting happens after the container has been built, this is now impossible. As an alternative, the script `install_clusterone_and_lazyfox.sh` now resides in that path. Running it will perform the same installation performed by the dockerfile. Run this script as needed.
